blocks.text: Third, as the serpent is crafty, Gen. III, 1., so the devil is by far the most cunning. Hence he is said to have seduced Eve ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτοῦ [en tē panourgia autou], 2 Cor. XI, 3. Fourth, as the poison of the serpent is spread through the whole body, so the poison of the demon is spread through the whole soul. Finally, nothing is more hateful to man than the serpent, nothing that we flee more.

[III, 239] Hence Theophrastus in the Characters, on cavilling: Τὰ δὴ τῶν ἠθῶν μὴ ἁπλᾶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπίβουλα, φυλάττεσθαι μᾶλλον δεῖ, ἢ τοὺς ἔχεις [Ta dē tōn ēthōn mē hapla, all᾽ epiboula, phylattesthai mallon dei, ē tous echeis]; Characters that are not simple but treacherous must be shunned more than vipers. And in Theocritus, Praxinoë, to show that she dreads above all horses that throw their riders, says:
Ἵππον, καὶ τὸν ψυχρὸν ὄφιν, τὰ μάλιστα δεδοίκω· [Hippon, kai ton psychron ophin, ta malista dedoikō;]
A horse and the cold snake I fear most. And Plautus in the Mercator:
Your wife, of course, is in the country, whom a while ago you said you hated as much as snakes. — —
As Horace in the first book of the Epistles:
— — he will shun it worse than a dog and a snake. — — —
So between the race of demons and that of men there is a bitter hatred, of which Gen. III, 15. speaks. But we touch on this only in passing, since these matters belong to another place.

[So that nothing that could be in any way useful and profitable should be missing from our edition of Bochart's work, it seemed good to append to this book, by way of a supplement, what Bochart discussed in vol. I, book I, Chapter IV on serpents in general, since it contains much that does not recur in the rest of the work, yet deserves not to be neglected by the interpreter of the O. T., especially of Chapter III of Genesis.]

The serpent is ζῶον ἑρπετὸν, ἔναιμον, φολιδωτὸν [zōon herpeton, enaimon, pholidōton], a creeping animal, endowed with blood, covered with scales. Its proper part is the גחון gachon, Gen. III, 14., that is, the elongated belly on which it creeps. The Philosopher ^{a)}: Τὴν δὲ κοιλίαν ὁ ὄφις ἔχει, οἷον ἔντερον εὐρυχωρέστερον [Tēn de koilian ho ophis echei, hoion enteron eurychōresteron]. There are those who think that the serpent at its creation was four-footed, or at least two-footed like dragons, and that its now creeping on its belly belongs to the punishment. But it does not seem likely to me that God changed anything in the nature of the serpent on account of man's sin. Only what belonged to its nature was turned into a punishment, as nakedness in man and childbirth in woman. Nor indeed is it sufficiently certain that any dragon is two-footed, or, as Pliny says ^{b)}, that serpents have been seen with goose's feet. Augustine, book 3 De Gen. ad lit., expressly asserts that dragons are without feet. And the Philosopher, in the book On the Progression of Animals, proves at length that neither two nor four feet could suffice a serpent because of the enormous length of its body, and that it could not have more, because τῶν ἐναίμων μηδὲν οἷον τ᾽ εἶναι πλείοσι σημείοις κινεῖσθαι, ἢ τέτταρσιν [tōn enaimōn mēden hoion t᾽ einai pleiosi sēmeiois kineisthai, ē tettarsin]. Hence he concludes that τὴν ἀποδίαν [tēn apodian] is necessary in the serpent.
